reason: This passage (2 Samuel 11-12) recounts David's adultery with Bathsheba and his subsequent murder of her husband Uriah. Critically, the text explicitly condemns these actions: 'And the thing that David did was evil in the sight of the Lord' (וַיֵּרַע הַדָּבָ֛ר אֲשֶׁר־ עָשָׂ֥ה דָוִ֖ד בְּעֵינֵ֥י יְהוָֽה). The narrative presents David's use of violence not as exemplary leadership, but as a moral transgression that requires prophetic condemnation (through Nathan), divine judgment ('the sword shall not depart from your house'), and royal repentance ('I have sinned against the Lord'). Uriah, the victim of David's violence, is portrayed as righteous and honorable, not unruly. The passage functions as a moral critique of power abuse, not as a leadership model to emulate.
